questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson describe permissionless blockchains as a dual-use environment rather than as simply anonymous criminal infrastructure?
questions.correct_answer: They allow open, borderless access that illicit actors can exploit, while public ledgers also preserve evidence investigators can later analyze.
incorrect_answers: They enforce strict cryptographic privacy at the consensus layer, while centralized nodes actively censor any transactions flagged by local regulators.
They mandate verified identity credentials for all basic actions, while native protocol gates prevent non-compliant entities from executing transfers.
They block suspicious transaction flows before they settle on-chain, while third-party compliance agencies retain unilateral control of every smart contract.
questions.explanation: The lesson's core framing is dual-use: weak base-layer identity checks and borderless settlement create risk, but immutable public records create durable forensic traces.

questions.question_stem: An investigator can see that one wallet cluster repeatedly receives ransomware proceeds, but has not yet linked the cluster to a person. Which concept best describes that situation?
questions.correct_answer: Pseudonymity: the address activity is persistent and traceable, but real-world attribution still requires additional evidence.
incorrect_answers: Anonymity: address activity disappears after each transfer, leaving no stable history for investigators to follow.
Custodial identity: the ledger lists wallet owners, making exchange records and seized devices unnecessary in every case.
Protocol attestation: every wallet signs a verified legal name into transfers, so attribution is automatic for analysts.
questions.explanation: Pseudonymous addresses can be tracked over time without automatically identifying a human operator. Attribution often needs exchange records, OSINT, subpoenas, seized devices, or other off-chain evidence.

questions.question_stem: A laundering path splits a large payment into many smaller transfers, routes some value through a mixer, and swaps the rest through a bridge into another asset. What is the best forensic interpretation?
questions.correct_answer: The actor is combining techniques that blur source, volume, and cross-chain continuity rather than relying on one method to erase the ledger.
incorrect_answers: The actor is executing atomic swaps to fully prevent off-chain tracking, rather than leaving decentralized protocols to record transaction details.
The actor is using privacy tools to delete historical ledger records entirely, rather than scattering pseudonymous balances across deposit addresses.
The actor relies on centralized custodians to completely hide cross-chain routes, rather than using smart contracts to automate asset settlement logs.
questions.explanation: Mixers, peel chains, layering, and chain hopping target different parts of the trail. They complicate source, path, volume, and continuity analysis, but do not delete historical ledger records.

questions.question_stem: A tracing team has a clean transaction graph showing funds moving from a theft address to an exchange deposit address. What would most directly move the investigation from tracing toward enforceable action?
questions.correct_answer: Exchange records, legal process, or other off-chain evidence that links the deposit account to an identity or controllable asset.
incorrect_answers: Automated tracking graphs, software telemetry, or other network analytics that show the transfer routing without linking to real identities.
Formal declarations, official assertions, or other public statements that label the receiving address as illicit without further evidence.
Privacy coin transfers, shielded transactions, or other zero-knowledge routing that bypasses traditional legal processes and boundaries.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that transaction traces become seizures, prosecutions, sanctions, or freezes only when combined with attribution, legal authority, jurisdiction, and sometimes key or account control.

questions.question_stem: Why can a CoinJoin-style transaction undermine a common-input-ownership heuristic?
questions.correct_answer: Multiple users may intentionally contribute inputs to one transaction, so shared inputs do not necessarily mean one owner controls all of them.
incorrect_answers: CoinJoin converts all inputs into private fiat balances during execution, so tracing tools cannot detect any later on-chain transaction activity.
Common-input ownership is absolute cryptographic proof, so coordinated users cannot affect its reliability in forensic review at all.
The heuristic applies only to cross-chain bridges and wrapped assets, so single-ledger transaction analysis needs no verification.
questions.explanation: Forensic heuristics are useful but fallible inference rules. Privacy tools can deliberately target those assumptions, creating false-positive risks if heuristics are treated as proof.

questions.question_stem: Which comparison best captures the lesson's distinction between centralized exchanges, DEXs, and bridges in laundering workflows?
questions.correct_answer: Centralized exchanges can create KYC and fiat off-ramp records, DEXs automate crypto-to-crypto swaps, and bridges move value across chain boundaries that require correlation.
incorrect_answers: Centralized exchanges publish identity profiles for users, DEXs require custodial registration, and bridges erase cross-chain transaction records after settlement.
Centralized exchanges operate as private mixers, DEXs serve as fiat cash-out chokepoints, and bridges identify users automatically during each swap event and report identities.
Centralized exchanges remove chain boundaries, DEXs maintain unified customer accounts, and bridges issue shared identifiers across every network in the route.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes chokepoints and trace surfaces: centralized exchanges may connect to accounts and fiat, DEXs reduce account-based intermediaries for crypto swaps, and bridges create cross-chain continuity challenges.

questions.question_stem: A bridge emits a withdrawal on Chain B minutes after a deposit on Chain A, with a fee-adjusted amount that closely matches the original transfer. Why is that useful for cross-chain tracing, and what remains unresolved?
questions.correct_answer: Bridge logs, timing, amount, and fee-adjusted matching can support transaction linkage across chains, but real-world identity attribution still needs corroborating evidence.
incorrect_answers: The matching amount and deposit sequence prove one identity controlled both wallets, while validators can still censor those funds before bridge exit records finalize.
The bridge event automatically files a suspicious activity report with regulators, though operators can erase every local bridge server record afterward quickly.
Cross-chain tracing is impossible once funds leave the primary ledger, but filters can still identify the initial transaction source with certainty afterward.
questions.explanation: The XSema-style slide supports automated cross-chain linkage from bridge logs, timing windows, and fee-adjusted amount matching. Separate attribution evidence is still needed before tying that linked flow to a human or organization.

questions.question_stem: A jurisdiction tightens exchange KYC rules, and laundering activity shifts toward weak foreign services, privacy assets, and direct crypto-denominated spending. What lesson concept does this illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Regulation can displace adversary behavior, so enforcement must account for jurisdictional arbitrage and no-cash-out economies.
incorrect_answers: Regulation stops illicit activity at domestic borders, so local enforcement can halt global laundering without foreign cooperation.
Regulation makes privacy coins fully untraceable for investigators, so authorities should ignore ledger data in active cases.
Regulation proves direct crypto spending is impossible on public ledgers, so every transfer must use domestic exchanges.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats regulation as part of a cat-and-mouse dynamic. Chokepoints matter, but adversaries adapt through weaker jurisdictions, privacy coins, decentralized tools, and spending without fiat conversion.

questions.question_stem: A proposed provenance-bearing chain would require valid custody proofs before accepting transfers. Which evaluation best matches the lesson's design tradeoff?
questions.correct_answer: It could improve auditability and compliance, but it would reduce privacy and permissionless access while adding consensus-enforced public-protocol constraints.
incorrect_answers: It would preserve complete public-chain anonymity and user sovereignty, but it would eliminate validator security controls while complicating protocol governance rules.
It would bypass subpoenas and warrants entirely, but automate criminal indictments while requiring a centralized identity database for every user.
It would completely fix validator key compromise on bridges, but restrict software upgrades while replacing decentralized token governance models entirely.
questions.explanation: Embedded provenance can attach origin, custody, and compliance context to transactions, but the visible slides frame that as a public-protocol tradeoff involving auditability, privacy, permissionless access, and consensus enforcement.

questions.question_stem: In the Colonial Pipeline case, why was following the ransom trail not enough by itself to recover funds?
questions.correct_answer: Recovery required tracing to intersect with jurisdiction, legal authority, and control over the relevant key or account.
incorrect_answers: Recovery succeeded once agents found the public ledger addresses and flagged the funds at several local exchanges.
Recovery failed because ransomware payments use encrypted assets that prevent investigators from tracing transactions.
Recovery depended entirely on proving a bridge smart contract contained a specific exploitable code bug in production networks.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses Colonial Pipeline to distinguish tracing from recovery: live transaction visibility mattered, but asset recovery depended on legal process and practical control.

questions.question_stem: Under the reading's summary of FinCEN's 2013 guidance, which actor is most likely to be treated as a money services business rather than an ordinary user?
questions.correct_answer: A business that accepts, transmits, buys, or sells convertible virtual currency for customers.
incorrect_answers: A person who buys virtual currency solely to purchase goods or services for personal use.
A wallet developer who publishes noncustodial code but never controls customer value.
A merchant who receives one virtual currency payment and records it as a routine sale.
questions.explanation: The CRS reading emphasizes FinCEN's functional distinction: ordinary users are generally not MSBs, while administrators and exchangers operating as businesses may be money transmitters.

questions.question_stem: The reading describes AML compliance as an institutional data-production system. Which scenario best illustrates that mechanism?
questions.correct_answer: An exchange maintains customer records, monitors suspicious behavior, and files reports that investigators can later use with transaction traces.
incorrect_answers: A public blockchain validates user passports, requires node administrator approval, and stores records developers can always access.
A protocol mixer deletes transaction histories, blocks institutional data collection, and prevents later agency search efforts entirely.
A federal court prosecutes ordinary crypto users, classifies private protocols as illegal, and issues globally binding orders for every ledger involved.
questions.explanation: The CRS report explains that covered institutions have AML programs, recordkeeping, and suspicious activity reporting duties. Those duties create off-chain evidence that can connect to pseudonymous flows.

questions.question_stem: Which policy argument best reflects the reading's treatment of legal uncertainty around virtual currency regulation?
questions.correct_answer: Clearer AML coverage can help enforcement, but broad or unclear duties may burden legitimate developers and noncustodial actors who do not control customer funds.
incorrect_answers: Legal uncertainty affects only underground marketplaces, but unclear rules may restrict retail purchases through privacy wallets and small exchanges.
Existing AML law cannot apply to virtual currencies without Congress, but courts may suspend tokens lacking legal tender status during agency reviews.
The Congressional report resolves the regulatory issue by treating all software publishers as custodial money transmitters, but it exempts noncustodial network validators.
questions.explanation: The CRS reading presents a tradeoff: regulators and prosecutors need workable legal categories, while overly broad obligations can chill innovation or sweep in actors without customer custody or control.
